candidates.label: Athens (historic center and Acropolis)
candidates.support: Athens is continuously inhabited and undisputed as the site of the New Testament city. Wikidata's point for the modern capital lies about 1.4 km from Pleiades' representative point for the ancient city, consistent with the two datasets marking slightly different reference features within the same urban area.

summary.text: Athens lay inland from its port of Piraeus, to which it had once been joined by long defensive walls, and was dominated by the Acropolis, a steep rock about 200 feet high at the city's center. By Paul's day Athens had lost its old political power but remained a celebrated center of art, philosophy, and learning under Roman rule. The Acropolis still carried its great fifth-century BC buildings nearly intact: the Propylaea gateway, the Parthenon with its gold-and-ivory statue of the goddess Athena by the sculptor Phidias, the Erechtheum, and the small temple of Athena Nike.

history.text: Acts describes Paul, troubled at seeing a city full of idols, reasoning daily in the marketplace, including with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers who called him a "babbler." They brought him to the Areopagus, where he told the Athenians, "I perceive that you are very religious in all things," and preached about an altar he had seen inscribed "TO AN UNKNOWN GOD." When he spoke of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked him, but a few believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris.

The great Temple of Olympian Zeus, whose foundations had been laid centuries earlier, stood unfinished in Paul's day; it was not completed until decades later, under the Roman emperor Hadrian, who placed his own statue inside it. Paul left Athens for Corinth after this single recorded visit, and no New Testament letter is addressed to the city.

Today Athens is the capital and largest city of Greece, built around the same Acropolis that stood in Paul's day. The Parthenon and the other Acropolis buildings survive, though in ruins, and the Agora below has been excavated to reveal the stoas and other public buildings Paul would have walked past.

scripture.textWEB: But those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens. Receiving a commandment to Silas and Timothy that they should come to him very quickly, they departed.
Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols.
So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who met him.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also were conversing with him. Some said, “What does this babbler want to say?” Others said, “He seems to be advocating foreign deities,” because he preached Jesus and the resurrection.
They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is, which you are speaking about?
Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing.
Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things.
For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, I announce to you.
Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, “We want to hear you again concerning this.”
But certain men joined with him and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
After these things Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth.
Therefore when we couldn’t stand it any longer, we thought it good to be left behind at Athens alone,
